question:
The given sentence is divided into four segments. Select the option that has the segment with a grammatical error.
Jerry driving / home late / when the incident / took place.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Jerry driving.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence is "Jerry driving / home late / when the incident / took place." This is meant to describe an ongoing action in the past (the Past Continuous Tense) that was interrupted by another action.

• Rule — Past Continuous Tense: Subject + was/were + V1+ing. The auxiliary verb "was/were" is compulsory before the "-ing" form of the main verb; the "-ing" form alone cannot function as the main verb of a sentence.

• In segment 3, "Jerry driving" is missing the auxiliary "was". It should read "Jerry was driving".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "took place." is grammatically correct — the Simple Past Tense "took place" correctly describes the completed action that interrupted the ongoing one.

• Option 2: "when the incident" is grammatically correct — it is simply a conjunction "when" joining the two clauses, with no verb error.

• Option 4: "home late" is grammatically correct — it is an adverbial phrase modifying the verb, with no error of its own.

NOTE

• Whenever a sentence describes an action that was in progress when another action interrupted it, use: Subject + was/were + V-ing ... + when/while + Subject + V2 (Simple Past).

• Common SSC trap: dropping "was/were" before a V-ing form, e.g. "She singing a song" (incorrect) vs "She was singing a song" (correct).

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Unfourseen.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling of the word is "Unforeseen" — not able to be foreseen or anticipated; unexpected. The option given, "Unfourseen", is misspelled because the letter combination "fore" has been wrongly written as "four".

• Spelling key: UN + FORE + SEEN. The prefix "fore-" means "before" (as in forecast, foretell, forewarn) and must never be replaced by the number word "four".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Possession" is correctly spelt — double "s" twice, meaning ownership or control of something.

• Option 3: "Referred" is correctly spelt — the final consonant "r" of "refer" is doubled before adding "-ed" because the stress falls on the last syllable.

• Option 4: "Weather" is correctly spelt — the atmospheric condition, spelt W-E-A-T-H-E-R, not to be confused with "whether".

NOTE

• Other "fore-" words commonly tested: forecast, foresee, forefather, forego, foremost, forewarn — never spelt with "four-".

• Do not confuse "weather" (atmospheric condition) with "whether" (conjunction expressing a choice/doubt) — a classic SSC homophone trap.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Evoke
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Induce.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Evoke" means to bring or recall a feeling, memory, or image to the conscious mind; to call forth or produce a reaction. (किसी भावना या स्मृति को जगाना)
◦ Example: The old photographs evoked many happy memories of childhood.

• "Induce" means to bring about or give rise to (a condition or state); to persuade or influence. It shares the core sense of "bringing about or calling forth" with "evoke", making it the closest synonym among the given options.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Abandon" (छोड़ देना): To give up completely or desert; it means the opposite kind of action and is unrelated to "evoke".

• Option 3: "Divert" (मोड़ना): To turn something aside from its course; it means to redirect, not to call forth a feeling.

• Option 4: "Reduce" (कम करना): To make something smaller in size, amount or degree; it has no connection with recalling or producing a feeling.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "evoke": arouse, elicit, stir, kindle, summon up.

• Do not confuse "evoke" with "invoke" — "invoke" means to call upon (a higher power, law, or authority) for help or support, e.g. "to invoke the law".

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the word in brackets to fill in the blanks.
The soldiers spent long period ________ (convalescing).
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. recovering.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Convalescing" means gradually recovering health and strength after an illness or medical treatment. (बीमारी के बाद स्वास्थ्य लाभ करना)
◦ Example: She spent two weeks convalescing at her aunt's house after the surgery.

• Among the given options, "recovering" carries the exact same meaning of gradually regaining health, making it the most appropriate synonym to fill the blank: "The soldiers spent long period recovering."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "attacking" (हमला करना): To act aggressively against someone or something; opposite in sense to healing/recovering.

• Option 2: "travelling" (यात्रा करना): To go from one place to another; unrelated to the idea of regaining health.

• Option 4: "ailing" (बीमार होना): To be in poor health or suffering from illness — this is nearly the opposite of "convalescing", which refers to the recovery phase after illness, not the illness itself.

NOTE

• Related words: convalescence (noun, the process of recovering), convalescent (adjective/noun, a person recovering from illness).

• Do not confuse "convalescing" (recovering) with "ailing" (being ill) — SSC frequently sets these as confusable distractors.

question: Select the correctly spelled sentence.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The restaurant serves delicious meals.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correctly spelt sentence is "The restaurant serves delicious meals." Both key words — "restaurant" (R-E-S-T-A-U-R-A-N-T) and "delicious" (D-E-L-I-C-I-O-U-S) — are spelt correctly here.

• Spelling key for "restaurant": it is a French loan word — remember the sequence "-au-" in the middle and the silent "-t" at the end. Spelling key for "delicious": remember the ending "-cious", not "-sious" or "-scious".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "The resturaunt serves delisious meals." — incorrect; "restaurant" is misspelt as "resturaunt" (the letters around "au" are jumbled) and "delicious" is misspelt as "delisious" (the "c" is wrongly replaced by "s").

• Option 3: "The resturant serves deliscious meals." — incorrect; "restaurant" is misspelt as "resturant" (missing the "au") and "delicious" is misspelt as "deliscious" (an extra "s" is inserted before "cious").

• Option 4: "The resteraunt serves delicious meals." — incorrect; "delicious" is spelt correctly here, but "restaurant" is misspelt as "resteraunt" (the "a" after "rest" is wrongly replaced by "e").

NOTE

• Other commonly misspelt words on this pattern: restaurant, delicious, precious, conscious, gracious, vicious — remember the "-cious" ending.

• Practice writing "restaurant" fully: R-E-S-T-A-U-R-A-N-T; the trickiest part is the "au" combination.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Intelligible
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Incoherent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Intelligible" means able to be understood; clear or comprehensible. (समझने योग्य, स्पष्ट)
◦ Example: His explanation was intelligible even to a young child.

• "Incoherent" means unclear and difficult to understand, especially because of a lack of logical connection, which is the direct opposite of "intelligible".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Scriptable": A technical term meaning capable of being controlled by a script (as in computing); it has no meaningful relationship with "intelligible" as an antonym.

• Option 2: "Embezzle" (गबन करना): To steal or misappropriate money placed in one's trust; completely unrelated in meaning.

• Option 4: "Deliberate" (जानबूझकर): Done consciously and intentionally; it is not an opposite of "intelligible" — a deliberate statement can still be perfectly intelligible.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "intelligible": comprehensible, clear, lucid, coherent, understandable.

• Other antonym pairs frequently tested: coherent × incoherent, lucid × obscure, comprehensible × unintelligible.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
The lions became violently / when the visitors / started throwing / stones at them.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The lions became violently.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "became" is a linking verb (verb of incomplete predication). A linking verb must be followed by a subject complement, which is an adjective or noun, and never by an adverb.

• Rule: Linking verbs (be, become, seem, appear, look, feel, taste, smell, sound, grow, turn, etc.) + adjective, not adverb.

• In segment 2, "violently" (an adverb) has been wrongly used after the linking verb "became". It should be the adjective "violent" — "The lions became violent."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "stones at them." is grammatically correct — it is simply the object of "throwing", with no error.

• Option 3: "started throwing" is grammatically correct — "start" is correctly followed by the gerund "throwing".

• Option 4: "when the visitors" is grammatically correct — it is a subordinate clause opener with no grammatical fault.

NOTE

• Common confusable pairs after linking verbs: "She looks beautiful" (not beautifully); "The soup tastes good" (not well); "He felt bad" (not badly, unless describing his sense of touch).

• Remember: after action verbs, use adverbs — e.g. "He ran quickly" — but after linking verbs, use adjectives — e.g. "He seemed quick-witted".

question:
Select the word which means the same as the group of words given.
Essence or main point of any passage, lecture or book
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Gist.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Gist" means the essence or main point of any passage, lecture, speech or book; the substance of a matter. (सार, मूल तत्व)
◦ Example: Please give me the gist of the report; I don't have time to read it fully.

• This one-word substitute exactly matches the given phrase "Essence or main point of any passage, lecture or book."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Significance" (महत्व): The importance or meaning of something; it refers to how important a thing is, not specifically to the condensed main point of a text.

• Option 3: "Meaning" (अर्थ): The sense conveyed by words in general; too broad and generic to be the precise one-word substitute intended here.

• Option 4: "Heart" (सार/केंद्र, used figuratively): Can loosely mean the "core" of something in informal usage, but it is not the standard one-word substitute tested by SSC for this definition.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes: Synopsis (a brief summary of a larger work), Précis (a concise summary retaining essential points), Abstract (a summary of a scientific/research paper).

• Do not confuse "gist" with "jist" — the correct spelling has a g, though it is pronounced with a soft "j" sound.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Grotesque
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Ugly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Grotesque" means comically or repulsively ugly or distorted in appearance. (भद्दा, विकृत)
◦ Example: The carved gargoyles on the old cathedral had grotesque faces.

• "Ugly" is the closest synonym, capturing the core meaning of being unpleasant or distorted in appearance.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Shameful" (शर्मनाक): Causing or deserving shame; relates to disgraceful conduct, not physical appearance.

• Option 2: "Comely" (सुंदर): Pleasant to look at, attractive — this is actually close to an antonym of "grotesque", not a synonym.

• Option 4: "Spontaneous" (सहज, स्वतःस्फूर्त): Done or occurring without planning; entirely unrelated to appearance or ugliness.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "grotesque": bizarre, distorted, misshapen, hideous, freakish.

• Antonyms of "grotesque": comely, graceful, elegant, beautiful — watch out for such antonym-as-distractor options in synonym questions.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Arushya purchased the most good of all the suits kept in the shop.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. the best.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence is "Arushya purchased the most good of all the suits kept in the shop." The underlined phrase "the most good" is an incorrect superlative form.

• Rule — Degrees of Comparison (irregular adjective): The adjective "good" has irregular comparative and superlative forms: good → better → best. It does NOT form its superlative by adding "most" before it.

• Since the sentence compares "of all the suits" (three or more items), the superlative degree is required, which for "good" is "best".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "the goods" is incorrect — this changes "good" into the noun "goods" (merchandise), which does not fit the intended meaning of "the best one".

• Option 3: "the more good" is incorrect — "more good" is an ungrammatical comparative form; the correct comparative of "good" is "better", and in any case the sentence needs the superlative, not the comparative.

• Option 4: "the good" is incorrect — the plain positive degree "good" cannot correctly replace a superlative sense of "the most good/best" required by "of all the suits".

NOTE

• Other common irregular degrees of comparison: bad → worse → worst; little → less → least; many/much → more → most; far → farther/further → farthest/furthest.

• Never use "more" or "most" together with an adjective that already has an irregular comparative/superlative form (e.g. "most best" or "more better" are always incorrect).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Loving
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Affectionate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Loving" means feeling or showing love and affection towards someone. (प्रेमपूर्ण, स्नेही)
◦ Example: She gave her children a loving smile before leaving for work.

• "Affectionate" means readily showing feelings of fondness or love, which is an exact match in meaning with "loving".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Subordinate" (अधीनस्थ): Lower in rank or position; relates to hierarchy, not emotion.

• Option 3: "Rejuvenate" (पुनर्जीवित करना): To make someone or something look or feel young, healthy, or energetic again; it is a verb about renewal, not love.

• Option 4: "Offish" (informal, short for "standoffish"): Reserved, distant, unfriendly — this is actually close to the opposite of "loving".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "loving": affectionate, fond, tender, warm, devoted, caring.

• Antonym of "loving": cold, indifferent, unaffectionate, offish.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the underlined group of words.
We, as human beings, have a tendency of believing in the things that can be seen and touched.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. tangible.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Tangible" means perceptible by touch; capable of being seen and touched; real or definite. (स्पर्शनीय, मूर्त)
◦ Example: The company showed tangible proof of its progress in the form of increased sales figures.

• This one-word substitute exactly matches the underlined phrase "things that can be seen and touched."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "impalpable" (अस्पष्ट, अगोचर): Unable to be felt by touch; not easily grasped by the mind — this is actually the opposite meaning of "tangible".

• Option 2: "spiritual" (आध्यात्मिक): Relating to the human spirit/soul rather than physical or material things; the opposite domain to something seen/touched.

• Option 3: "inexpressible" (अवर्णनीय): Too great or intense to be described in words; unrelated to physical perceptibility.

NOTE

• Antonym of "tangible": intangible (something that cannot be touched, e.g. "intangible assets" like goodwill or reputation).

• Related one-word substitutes: Palpable (that can be touched or felt; obvious), Perceptible (able to be perceived by the senses).

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom to fill in the blank.
After months of dedication and effort, I finally completed the marathon. I can really ________________ for this accomplishment.
option_2: up a creek without a paddle
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. pat myself on the back.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to pat oneself on the back" means to praise or congratulate oneself for an achievement. (अपनी पीठ थपथपाना, स्वयं की प्रशंसा करना)
◦ Example: After winning the contract, he patted himself on the back for closing such a big deal.

• The sentence describes the speaker completing a marathon after months of dedication — a personal achievement worth self-congratulation — which fits this idiom perfectly: "I can really pat myself on the back for this accomplishment."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "eat like a horse" (बहुत ज्यादा खाना): To eat a large amount of food; unrelated to the context of completing an achievement.

• Option 2: "up a creek without a paddle" (मुश्किल में फंसना): To be in a difficult situation with no clear way out; the context here is one of success, not difficulty.

• Option 3: "blow hot and cold" (कभी हां कभी ना करना): To keep changing one's opinion or attitude about something; does not fit a context of celebrating an accomplishment.

NOTE

• Other idioms of self-praise/achievement: "a feather in one's cap" (an achievement to be proud of), "take a bow" (to accept praise/applause for one's achievement).

• Other idioms of difficulty, often confused with "up a creek without a paddle": "between the devil and the deep sea", "caught between a rock and a hard place".

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom in the following sentence.
The leader of the Legislative Assembly won the hearts of the members through his maiden speech during the session in state council.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. first speech.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "maiden speech" means the first speech given by a person, especially by a newly elected member in a legislative body such as a parliament or assembly. (पहला भाषण)
◦ Example: The newly elected MP was visibly nervous while delivering her maiden speech in Parliament.

• In the given sentence, "his maiden speech during the session in state council" refers to the leader's very first speech in that assembly, matching Option 3.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "final speech": Means the last speech someone gives, which is the opposite of "maiden" (first).

• Option 2: "closure speech": Refers to a concluding speech that ends a session or debate, not a first speech.

• Option 4: "logical speech": Refers to a speech that is reasoned or coherent in argument, which has no connection to the idiom "maiden speech".

NOTE

• The word "maiden" as an adjective generally means "first" or "earliest", as also seen in expressions like "maiden voyage" (a ship's first official journey) and "maiden over" (in cricket, an over in which no runs are scored).

• Do not confuse "maiden speech" (first speech) with "farewell speech" (a speech given while leaving/departing).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Even if you've never heard his name, you've probably met someone with his words tattooed in their skin or heard them sung at a music concert.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. tattooed on their skin.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence uses the underlined phrase "tattooed in their skin", which is grammatically incorrect because of a wrong preposition.

• Rule — Preposition usage: The verb "tattoo", when referring to a design permanently marked upon the surface of the skin, is idiomatically followed by the preposition "on", not "in", "until", or "overdoing". A tattoo sits on the surface of the skin.

• Applying the rule, the correct phrase is "tattooed on their skin".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "tattooed through their skin" is incorrect — "through" suggests passing all the way across/inside the skin, which is not the intended meaning.

• Option 2: "tattooed until their skin" is incorrect — "until" is a preposition/conjunction of time, and makes no logical sense here.

• Option 3: "tattooed overdoing their skin" is incorrect — "overdoing" is not a preposition at all and makes the sentence ungrammatical and meaningless.

NOTE

• Other fixed preposition combinations frequently tested by SSC: "written on paper", "printed on the cover", "engraved on stone/metal", "painted on canvas" — the surface on which a mark is made is generally introduced by "on".

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
A. at the same time giving happiness to the poor
B. by providing them with food, clothes, money or grain
C. festivals in India are celebrated to share happiness
D. by being in the presence of the members of the family and
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. CDAB.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correctly arranged sentence is: "Festivals in India are celebrated to share happiness by being in the presence of the members of the family and at the same time giving happiness to the poor by providing them with food, clothes, money or grain."

• Approach for parajumbles: Identify the part that can independently stand as the opening statement/main clause (here, C: "festivals in India are celebrated to share happiness", since it introduces the subject and the main idea). Then look for connecting words like "and" at the end of a part, which signals the next part must continue that same idea — D ends with "and", so it links directly to A, which continues with "at the same time giving happiness...". Finally, B logically explains "how" happiness is given to the poor, i.e., "by providing them with..." — coming right after A's "giving happiness to the poor".

• Sequence: C (main idea) → D (first means: family) → A (second means: the poor, joined by "and") → B (how: providing food etc.).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: ACBD is incorrect — it starts with "A" ("at the same time..."), which cannot be the opening part since it depends on an idea introduced earlier ("at the same time as what?").

• Option 2: CBAD is incorrect — placing B ("by providing them with food...") immediately after C breaks the logical link between D (family) and A (poor), and ends the sentence awkwardly on "and" (D).

• Option 3: CABD is incorrect — it places A right after C, but A ("at the same time giving happiness to the poor") needs D ("...and being in the presence of...") to logically precede it as the connecting phrase; also, ending on D ("and") leaves the sentence incomplete.

NOTE

• In parajumble questions, always scan for linking words ("and", "but", "which", "who", pronouns) at the start or end of each part — they are the strongest clues to correct sequencing.

• The part introducing the subject/main clause (without a dangling pronoun or connective) is almost always the correct opening part.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
The chef prepares the meal with great care.
option_1: The meal was prepared with great care by the chef.
option_2: The meal will be prepared with great care by the chef.
option_3: The meal is prepared with great care by the chef.
option_4: The meal has been prepared with great care by the chef.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The meal is prepared with great care by the chef.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The chef prepares the meal with great care" is an assertive sentence in the Simple Present Tense.

• Rule — Simple Present Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V1/V5 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + is/am/are + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the meal" becomes the subject; being singular, the auxiliary used is "is"; the verb "prepares" becomes the past participle "prepared"; and "the chef" becomes the agent introduced by "by".
◦ Passive: The meal is prepared with great care by the chef.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "was prepared" is the passive form of the Simple Past Tense, not the Simple Present Tense used in the original sentence.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "will be prepared" is the passive form of the Simple Future Tense.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "has been prepared" is the passive form of the Present Perfect Tense.

NOTE

• The adverbial phrase "with great care" remains unchanged in its position between the verb and the agent when converting to the passive voice.

• Always identify the tense of the active sentence first, since the auxiliary verb used in the passive voice depends entirely on that tense.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Necessary
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Essential.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Necessary" means required to be done, achieved, or present; needed; indispensable. (आवश्यक)
◦ Example: It is necessary to carry a valid ID card while appearing for the exam.

• "Essential" means absolutely necessary; extremely important, which is an exact synonym of "necessary".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Potential" (संभावित): Having the capacity to develop into something in the future; refers to possibility, not requirement.

• Option 3: "Existential" (अस्तित्व संबंधी): Relating to existence, particularly human existence; a philosophical term unrelated to necessity.

• Option 4: "Spatial" (स्थानिक): Relating to space or the position, area, and size of things; unrelated in meaning to "necessary".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "necessary": essential, indispensable, requisite, imperative, vital.

• Antonym of "necessary": unnecessary, optional, dispensable, needless.

question:
Select the option that expresses the following sentence in active voice.
The novels of Dickens are being read by Mayank.
option_1: Mayank is reading the novels of Dickens.
option_2: Mayank has been reading the novels of Dickens.
option_3: Mayank was reading the novels of Dickens.
option_4: Mayank had been reading the novels of Dickens.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Mayank is reading the novels of Dickens.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The novels of Dickens are being read by Mayank" is a passive sentence in the Present Continuous Tense.

• Rule — Present Continuous Tense:
◦ Passive: Object + is/am/are + being + V3 + by + Subject
◦ Active: Subject + is/am/are + V1+ing + Object

• Applying the rule: the agent "Mayank" (introduced by "by") becomes the subject; the auxiliary "is" is retained (since Mayank is singular/third person); "being read" is converted to the present participle "reading"; and "the novels of Dickens" becomes the object.
◦ Active: Mayank is reading the novels of Dickens.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "has been reading" is the active form of the Present Perfect Continuous Tense, not the Present Continuous Tense of the original passive sentence.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "was reading" is the active form of the Past Continuous Tense.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "had been reading" is the active form of the Past Perfect Continuous Tense.

NOTE

• In converting passive to active voice, the agent introduced by "by" in the passive sentence always becomes the subject of the active sentence, and vice versa.

• Recognise the Present Continuous passive pattern "is/am/are + being + V3" — it always converts to "is/am/are + V-ing" in the active voice.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
Fear of snakes
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Ophidiophobia.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Ophidiophobia" means an extreme or irrational fear of snakes. (सांपों का भय)
◦ Example: Her ophidiophobia was so severe that she could not even look at pictures of snakes.

• This one-word substitute exactly matches the given phrase "Fear of snakes."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Claustrophobia" (बंद स्थान का भय): An extreme fear of confined or enclosed spaces, not of snakes.

• Option 2: "Syngenesophobia": An extreme fear of one's relatives, unrelated to snakes.

• Option 3: "Xenophobia" (विदेशियों/अजनबियों का भय): An intense dislike or fear of strangers or foreigners, not of snakes.

NOTE

• Other commonly asked "-phobia" words: Acrophobia (fear of heights), Arachnophobia (fear of spiders), Claustrophobia (fear of enclosed spaces), Hydrophobia (fear of water), Nyctophobia (fear of darkness).

• The Greek root "ophis" means "snake", giving us "ophidiophobia" (fear of snakes) and "ophiology" (the scientific study of snakes).

Listening starts with hearing but goes (1)___________. Hearing, in other words, is necessary, but is not a sufficient (2)___________ for listening. Listening involves hearing with attention. Listening is a process that (3)___________ concentration. While listening, one should also be observant. In other words, listening has to do with the ears, (4)___________ with the eyes and the mind. Listening is to be understood as the total process that involves hearing with attention, being observant and making interpretations. Good communication is essentially a/an (5)___________ process.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. beyond.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "Listening starts with hearing but goes beyond [hearing]." This means that listening is not the same as hearing — it starts with hearing but extends further than mere hearing, requiring attention and interpretation as well.

• "Beyond" means further on or outside the limits of something, which correctly conveys the idea that listening is a more advanced process than hearing alone.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "towards" is incorrect — it would suggest listening moves "in the direction of" hearing, whereas the passage actually contrasts listening as something that surpasses/exceeds mere hearing.

• Option 2: "across" is incorrect — it does not logically fit the idea of listening extending further than hearing; "across" suggests movement from one side to another, not "surpassing a limit".

• Option 4: "throughout" is incorrect — it means "all through" or "during the entire period of" something, which does not fit the sense of listening exceeding the scope of hearing.

NOTE

• The passage's central theme is the distinction between "hearing" (a passive physical process) and "listening" (an active process requiring attention). Keeping this contrast in mind helps in choosing the correct connecting word for each blank.

• "Beyond" is commonly used in this comparative sense: "His talent goes beyond music; he is also a fine painter."

In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option, in the questions that follow, to fill in each blank.

Listening starts with hearing but goes (1)___________. Hearing, in other words, is necessary, but is not a sufficient (2)___________ for listening. Listening involves hearing with attention. Listening is a process that (3)___________ concentration. While listening, one should also be observant. In other words, listening has to do with the ears, (4)___________ with the eyes and the mind. Listening is to be understood as the total process that involves hearing with attention, being observant and making interpretations. Good communication is essentially a/an (5)___________ process.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. condition.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "Hearing, in other words, is necessary, but is not a sufficient condition for listening." This is a standard collocation in English — something is described as a "necessary condition" or a "sufficient condition" for something else to occur.

• "Condition" here means a requirement or circumstance that must be fulfilled for something to happen; the passage states hearing is required (necessary) but, by itself, is not enough (sufficient) for listening to take place.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "place" does not fit — the standard fixed expression is "necessary/sufficient condition", not "necessary/sufficient place".

• Option 2: "decorum" means proper or polite behaviour, which is unrelated to the logical relationship being described between hearing and listening.

• Option 4: "scenario" means a possible sequence of events or a setting/situation, which does not fit the fixed logical-relationship phrase "necessary but not sufficient condition".

NOTE

• "Necessary condition" vs "sufficient condition" is a common logical expression: a necessary condition must be present for something to occur, but its presence alone does not guarantee that the thing will occur (that would need a sufficient condition too).

• Watch for such fixed collocations in cloze passages — the correct option is often the one that forms a standard, natural English phrase.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

• Option 2: "disposes of" means "to get rid of" or "to deal with and finish a matter", which does not fit the meaning of "requiring" concentration.

• Option 4: "brings up" means "to raise a topic" or "to rear/bring up a child"; it does not carry the sense of "requiring" something.

NOTE

• "Calls for" is a commonly tested phrasal verb meaning "to require, demand, or need", e.g. "This situation calls for immediate action."

• Related phrasal verbs of "requiring": "call for", "ask for", "demand", "necessitate".

Listening is a process that (3)___________ concentration. While listening, one should also be observant. In other words, listening has to do with the ears, (4)___________ with the eyes and the mind. Listening is to be understood as the total process that involves hearing with attention, being observant and making interpretations. Good communication is essentially a/an (5)___________ process.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. as well as.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "listening has to do with the ears, as well as with the eyes and the mind." "As well as" is used to add an additional element to a list, meaning "in addition to; and also".

• Here it correctly connects "the ears" with the additional elements "the eyes and the mind", showing that listening involves all three, not just the ears.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "although" is a conjunction of contrast/concession, which would wrongly suggest an opposition between "the ears" and "the eyes and mind", whereas the sentence intends an addition, not a contrast.

• Option 2: "rather" typically signals a correction or preference between two alternatives ("rather than"), which does not fit the additive sense required here.

• Option 4: "yet" is a conjunction of contrast (similar to "but"), which is inappropriate since the sentence is adding related ideas, not contrasting them.

NOTE

• "As well as" is used to add extra information, similar in function to "in addition to" and "along with" — e.g. "She is intelligent as well as hardworking."

• Do not confuse additive connectors (as well as, along with, in addition to) with contrastive connectors (although, yet, but, however) in cloze passages — always check whether the sentence is adding or contrasting ideas.

solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. interactive.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "Good communication is essentially a/an interactive process." "Interactive" means involving communication or participation between two or more parties; acting on or influencing each other.

• Since the whole passage explains that listening (a two-way, participatory activity involving hearing, attention, observation and interpretation) is central to communication, describing communication as "interactive" logically concludes the passage.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "onerous" means "involving heavy duties or responsibilities; burdensome", which does not fit the concluding idea about communication being a two-way process.

• Option 2: "obnoxious" means "extremely unpleasant, causing strong dislike or disapproval"; it carries a negative connotation entirely unrelated to the passage's neutral, explanatory tone about communication.

• Option 4: "pecuniary" means "relating to or consisting of money"; it has no connection to the description of communication as a process involving listening and interpretation.

NOTE

• "a/an" before the blank signals that the correct option's first sound determines the article — "an interactive" (vowel sound) is grammatically consistent with "an".

• Communication is often described in exams as a two-way / interactive process, distinguishing it from a one-way transmission of information.
